# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) that develops toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause [1]. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group defines PPCM as heart failure occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, with an LVEF generally below 45% [2]. It remains an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide and represents a diagnostic challenge given the overlap of its symptoms with normal late pregnancy [3].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography, ranging from approximately 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 4,000 live births in the United States, to as high as 1 in 100 in parts of Nigeria and 1 in 300 in Haiti [4,5]. Recognized risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, preeclampsia and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and African ancestry [6,7]. Registry data from the EORP PPCM registry have highlighted substantial regional differences in presentation, treatment, and outcomes [8].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but is increasingly attributed to a "two-hit" model combining systemic and genetic susceptibility with the hormonal environment of late pregnancy [9]. A central mechanism involves oxidative stress leading to cleavage of the nursing hormone prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic and proapoptotic fragment, which exerts deleterious effects on the cardiac microvasculature [10]. Reduced expression of cardioprotective STAT3 has been linked to this cascade in experimental models [10]. Additionally, the antiangiogenic factor soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) released from the placenta contributes to vascular damage, providing a mechanistic link with preeclampsia [11]. Genetic factors are also important: truncating variants in TTN (titin) and other cardiomyopathy genes are found in a significant minority of patients, suggesting shared genetic architecture with dilated cardiomyopathy [12,13].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

Patients typically present with dyspnea, fatigue, peripheral edema, and orthopnea, symptoms that may be mistaken for normal physiological changes of pregnancy [3]. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of heart failure and confirmation of left ventricular systolic dysfunction by echocardiography [2]. Natriuretic peptides (BNP or NT-proBNP) are elevated and assist in distinguishing PPCM from physiological dyspnea [14]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging can aid in characterizing myocardial involvement and excluding alternative diagnoses, though gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy [15]. Electrocardiographic abnormalities are common but nonspecific [16].

## Management

Management of PPCM follows standard heart failure guidelines, with modifications for pregnancy and lactation [2,17]. In women who remain pregnant, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated; beta-blockers (preferably beta-1 selective) and hydralazine with nitrates are preferred [17]. After delivery, guideline-directed medical therapy including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists should be initiated [18]. Anticoagulation is warranted because of the heightened thromboembolic risk, particularly with severely reduced LVEF [19].

Bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 receptor agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion, has emerged as a disease-specific therapy targeting the prolactin pathway [20]. A proof-of-concept trial and the larger German multicenter study demonstrated improved recovery of LV function with bromocriptine added to standard therapy [21]. The ESC recommends consideration of bromocriptine with concurrent anticoagulation [2]. For patients with advanced disease, mechanical circulatory support and cardiac transplantation may be necessary [22]. Wearable cardioverter-defibrillators have a role in protecting against sudden death during the period of potential recovery [23].

## Prognosis and Outcomes

PPCM carries a more favorable prognosis than many other cardiomyopathies, with a substantial proportion of women recovering LV function, often within 6–12 months [24]. The IPAC study reported recovery of LVEF in approximately 70% of women, with baseline LVEF and LV dimensions being key predictors [25]. Nonetheless, mortality remains significant, and outcomes are worse in low-resource settings and among Black women [26,27]. Persistent LV dysfunction is associated with adverse long-term outcomes [28].

## Subsequent Pregnancies

Subsequent pregnancy poses a considerable risk of relapse, particularly in women whose LV function has not normalized [29]. Counseling regarding contraception and the risks of future pregnancy is an essential component of care, and women with persistent dysfunction should be strongly advised against further pregnancies [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a potentially life-threatening but often reversible cardiomyopathy. Advances in understanding the prolactin-mediated pathophysiology have informed disease-specific therapy with bromocriptine, while contemporary registries continue to refine our understanding of outcomes. Early recognition, multidisciplinary management, and careful counseling regarding future pregnancies remain central to improving maternal outcomes.
